questions.q: In ELT, what changes about the order of transform and load compared to traditional ETL?
options: Data is loaded raw first, then transformed afterward with SQL inside the warehouse
Data is transformed twice, once before and once after loading
Loading is skipped entirely
Extraction happens after transformation
questions.explain: ELT extracts, loads the raw data as-is, and only then transforms it — the opposite order from ETL, which transforms before loading.

questions.q: Why does Snowflake's architecture make ELT the natural pattern rather than ETL?
options: Storage and compute are billed and scaled separately, so loading raw data is cheap and transformation runs as ordinary SQL against a warehouse sized for the job
Snowflake cannot run transformations in SQL at all
Snowflake requires a separate transformation engine outside the warehouse
Snowflake charges more for storage than compute, making ETL cheaper
questions.explain: Because storage and compute costs are decoupled, landing raw data is inexpensive, and transformation is just SQL run against a right-sized, suspendable warehouse — no separate engine needed.

questions.q: What are the three logical layers this chapter and the next one build data through?
options: Raw, staging/cleaned, and business-ready
Bronze, silver, and gold only as Databricks terms with no Snowflake equivalent
Extract, transform, and archive
Development, testing, and production environments
questions.explain: The convention used throughout this chapter and Chapter 6 is raw (unmodified landing), staging/cleaned (typed and validated), and business-ready (modeled for BI).

questions.q: Why are transient tables a good fit for the raw and staging layers?
options: They skip the extra fail-safe recovery period, lowering storage cost for data that's fully reproducible by re-running the load or transform
They are the only table type that supports COPY INTO
They automatically enforce data quality rules
They cannot be queried with standard SELECT statements
questions.explain: Transient tables drop the fail-safe period permanent tables carry, which is appropriate for raw/staging data since it can always be rebuilt from the source or the prior layer.

questions.q: Why is the business-ready layer usually made up of permanent tables instead of transient ones?
options: Reports depend on it directly, and rebuilding it may be expensive or slow, so the extra recovery protection is worth the cost
Permanent tables are always cheaper to store than transient tables
Business-ready tables cannot legally be transient in Snowflake
Permanent tables load data faster than transient tables
questions.explain: Because business-ready data is what downstream reports rely on and may be costly to rebuild, the fail-safe protection permanent tables provide is usually worth paying for.
